faq.question: Can Qwen Image 3.0 generate uncensored NSFW images?
faq.answer: Yes. There is no content filter, no maturity flag and no separate endpoint for it — uncensored prompts go to the same text-to-image and image-to-image endpoints as everything else.

faq.question: How much text can it actually render inside an image?
faq.answer: Qwen’s 3.0 announcement covers complex layouts and fine text, not an eight-word ceiling; the SpicyAPI examples here concentrate on signs and labels, so proofread the actual wording and layout you receive.

faq.question: What is the difference between the 1k and 2k tiers?
faq.answer: resolution picks the output tier and it is the tier choice that changes the price; on image editing each reference image also adds to the quote. 2k is the default and the one that keeps small type and fine texture; 1k is for fast layout roughs.

faq.question: How many images can one request return?
faq.answer: One. num_outputs is fixed at 1, so each request returns a single image and is quoted and settled on its own. For several draws of one brief, send parallel requests without a seed.

faq.question: How is image-to-image different from text-to-image?
faq.answer: Image editing adds a required image_urls array of one to three sources and keeps every other field. Say in the prompt which reference contributes what; the model does not assign roles for you.

faq.question: Does it read prompts in Chinese?
faq.answer: Yes, natively, and there is no language parameter to set. The 5,000-character budget is the same either way, as is the way quoted strings are handled.

faq.question: Does Qwen Image 3.0 reproduce an image from its seed?
faq.answer: Use seed in Qwen Image 3.0 for controlled comparisons of signs and lettering in a scene; save the chosen image itself because a matching seed does not guarantee identical pixels.

faq.question: What does negative_prompt do that the prompt cannot?
faq.answer: It carries exclusions in a separate 2,000-character field, so the main prompt stays a description of what you want. Useful for suppressing watermarks, extra limbs and stray text.

howTo.title: Pin the seed, then vary one field
howTo.body: When a draw works, record its seed and change one field at a time from there. When you want variety instead, leave the seed out and send several requests in parallel; each returns one image and is quoted on its own.

familyContent.closing: Qwen Image 3.0 is Alibaba's Qwen image model, published here as two endpoints: text-to-image, and image-to-image that reads one to three reference images. Both take a prompt of up to 5,000 characters plus a 2,000-character negative prompt, eight aspect ratios, a 1k or 2k resolution tier, an optional seed, and num_outputs fixed at 1, billed per output image with reference images priced into image editing. Its distinguishing capability is legible in-image typography — signage, mastheads, packaging copy — and it runs uncensored, with no maturity flag and no prompt scanner in front of it.

data.readme:
Qwen Image 3.0 text-to-image is Alibaba's text-rendering model: quoted signage and headlines come back as readable type at the 2k tier. It takes 5,000-character prompts and a separate negative prompt, in eight aspect ratios at 1k or 2k.

### Signage and labels come back spelled right

Most image models turn quoted text into letter-shaped noise. Qwen Image 3.0 renders it: a brass door hanger reading DO NOT DISTURB, a bar sign, a bottle label, a poster headline. Put the wording in single quotes, keep it under about eight words per element, and generate at the 2k tier so the strokes survive.

### Add or retype lettering without redrawing the frame

The image-to-image endpoint writes onto surfaces that are already in the picture: letters drawn through fogged glass, lipstick on a mirror, a new line on an existing sign. Quote the wording, fence the edit to one area and say that everything else stays put, and the pose, light and grade come back as they were while only the words change.

### Uncensored scenes run on the same two endpoints

Fashion editorial and bold wording in the prompt are not routed anywhere special and do not need a flag. There is no per-request content declaration and no prompt scanner in front of the model. The only inputs that matter are the ones in the schema on this page.

### Hospitality and set-dressing plates

Hotel rooms, bars and lobbies where a specific sign has to read correctly: door hangers, room numbers, cocktail menus, neon above the back bar. Generate the plate with the wording already in place instead of compositing type over a render afterwards.

### Character sets and fashion series

Wardrobe and styling prompts that other image APIs bounce run here without a flag. Pin the seed that gave you the character, then change one detail per request — wardrobe, light, pose — for a coherent set rather than a pile of unrelated draws.

### Poster and packaging comps

Headline, subhead and a legal line, all rendered in the frame at 2k, in the ratio the placement actually uses. Useful for pitching a layout before a designer sets real type over a clean plate.

### Localised copy variants

Send the approved frame to the editing endpoint and change only the words on the sign. The pose, wardrobe, lighting and grade are described as unchanged, so the variant differs in the copy rather than in the whole picture.

### Choose the ratio and the tier first

aspect_ratio composes the frame, it does not crop one, so pick the shape you will publish at. Leave resolution at 2k whenever the image contains text; drop to 1k only for layout roughs where nothing has to be readable.

### Write the scene and quote the wording verbatim

Describe subject, wardrobe, light and lens, then put the exact string in single quotes. The still on this page came from: "Editorial photograph, an adult woman sitting on a hotel bed in a navy satin slip dress, city lights blurred through the window behind her, a brass door hanger hanging in sharp foreground reading 'DO NOT DISTURB', warm tungsten bedside lamp, cinematic 35mm, shallow focus, moody blue and amber palette."

### Pin the seed, then vary one field

When a draw works, record its seed and change one field at a time from there. When you want variety instead, leave the seed out and send several requests in parallel; each returns one image and is quoted on its own.

Qwen’s 3.0 announcement covers complex layouts and fine text, not an eight-word ceiling; the SpicyAPI examples here concentrate on signs and labels, so proofread the actual wording and layout you receive.

The prompt has to name which reference supplies what; with two or three sources the model does not infer roles on its own. Editing text in place works when you spell out both the old and the new wording. Identity drifts across heavy edits, so change one thing per pass rather than restyling and retyping in the same call.

For edits made with Qwen Image 3.0, use images you have permission to transform and publish, obtain adult participants’ consent, and avoid deceptive impersonation; these duties apply to signs and lettering in a scene even without request screening.

### `aspect_ratio`

Composes the frame before generation rather than cropping afterwards, so choose the shape the image will be published at. All eight ratios cost the same per image.

### `enable_prompt_expansion`

With Qwen Image 3.0, prompt expansion rewrites the instruction before rendering; for signs and lettering in a scene, compare the rewritten interpretation with your original brief rather than assuming the wording is preserved.

### `negative_prompt`

Up to 2,000 characters of exclusions, kept out of the main prompt. Worth spending on watermarks, duplicated limbs and garbled lettering when a frame carries type.

### `num_outputs`

Fixed at 1: each request returns one image. For a contact sheet from one brief, send parallel requests without a seed; each is quoted and settled on its own.

### `prompt`

Up to 5,000 characters, Chinese or English, no language flag. Put every string that must appear in the picture inside single quotes and keep each one to roughly eight words.

### `resolution`

For signs and lettering in a scene, Qwen Image 3.0 exposes 1k, 2k; the tier changes the quote, and editing references add to it

### `seed`

Omit it while exploring and every call draws its own. Fix it once a frame works, then change one other field at a time to see what each change did.

### `prompt_optimization_mode`

For signs and lettering in a scene in Qwen Image 3.0, prompt_optimization_mode accepts direct; this control only has an effect while prompt expansion is enabled.

The exact request behind the still on this page: a 3:4 hotel scene at the 2k tier with the door-hanger wording quoted in the prompt.

The exact request behind the second frame on this page — no quoted text in it at all, which is the fair test of whether the model still holds humid light and foliage detail when typography is not doing the work.

Handwriting rather than signage: two lines of looping fountain-pen ink on a folded card, held razor-sharp in the only plane in focus while the rest of the bed falls away. Quoting the exact words and describing the pen is what keeps them from turning into decorative squiggles.

Harder than a carved sign: the string is chalk handwriting on wet glass, so the letterforms are irregular by design and there is no clean baseline to snap to, and it still has to spell what the brief asked for. `resolution` is `2k`. The glass also gives the frame two depth planes - writing on the outside surface, a figure and a lit bottle behind it - which is what stops the handwriting from reading as a flat overlay.

The carved sign is named as an exact string in the brief and has to come back spelled the way it was asked for, on a surface that is simultaneously being lit and weathered. `resolution` is `2k`: at the lower tier the lettering tends to survive as shapes but loses the carved edge that makes it read as a sign rather than as a decal. The rest of the frame is one candle, so the type sits at the darkest end of the exposure.

input.prompt: Cinematic film still, medieval tavern barber under a carved wooden sign. The barber leans in with a straight razor while the customer tips his head fully back, the whole line of his throat exposed, lather bright under a single candle; the carved sign above reads THE BRASS COCK in clean lettering. Smoke and low beams behind. 35mm, shallow depth of field, heavy grain, candle amber and oak brown, restrained and tasteful.

The glass also gives the frame two depth planes - writing on the outside surface, a figure and a lit bottle behind it - which is what stops the handwriting from reading as a flat overlay.

input.prompt: Cinematic film still, an apothecary shop window at night. Chalk handwriting on the glass reads TODAY'S DRAUGHT - MOONWELL; behind it a woman tilts a glowing potion bottle, one camisole strap slipped to her elbow, the liquid's green light thrown up under her jaw. Rain beads on the outside of the glass. 35mm, shallow depth of field, heavy grain, potion green against night blue, restrained and tasteful.

input.prompt: Fashion editorial photograph shot inside a humid Victorian glasshouse. An adult woman in an emerald bandeau bikini top and a sheer chiffon sarong knotted low on one hip stands among giant monstera leaves, one hand parting a frond, condensation fogging the glass panes behind her. Cool green ambient light cut by a single warm shaft from a broken pane, medium-format sharpness, magazine crop, botanical detail.

examples.note: Handwriting rather than signage: two lines of looping fountain-pen ink on a folded card, held razor-sharp in the only plane in focus while the rest of the bed falls away. Quoting the exact words and describing the pen is what keeps them from turning into decorative squiggles.

input.prompt: Editorial photograph shot from a steep high angle, warm tungsten bedside lamp the only light source. A hotel nightstand and the corner of a rumpled bed: a folded cream card is propped against the lamp base, handwritten in looping blue fountain-pen ink, the first line reading 'WAKE ME' and the second line reading 'BEFORE YOU GO'. Beside the card sit a single dropped earring, a brass room key and a glass with a lipstick mark on the rim. Behind, thrown out of focus, an adult woman lies face-down across white sheets, bare back and shoulders, the sheet pulled up across her hips, one arm reaching toward the nightstand. Shallow focus holding the card razor sharp, warm amber highlights and deep shadow, 50mm, fine film grain. The handwriting is neat, evenly spaced and clearly legible.

Golden-hour balcony in a pastel seaside town: a handwritten note pinned under a lemon on the iron rail reads 'Same café, 8 pm?' in looping blue ink, and far below an adult man looks up from the street holding a bunch of wildflowers. Warm backlight, shallow depth of field, editorial film look.

Vintage screen-printed travel poster for a colony on a ringed planet: a silver rocket tram crossing a canyon under two moons, flat 1960s colours with visible paper texture, and bold lettering that reads 'VISIT THE RINGS' with a smaller line 'EXPRESS EVERY DAWN'.

A round ginger cat asleep on the counter of a tiny cluttered bookshop at dusk, beside a brass bell and a hand-lettered card that reads 'Shop cat on duty — please do not wake'. Warm lamplight, dust floating in the air, stacks of old books, cozy detail.
